title: Colorectal Polyp Follow-Up: Pathology, Number, Size, and Exam Quality Set the Interval
bottomLine: Post-polypectomy surveillance is not one universal 'repeat in five years' rule. The interval depends on polyp histology, number, size, completeness of resection, bowel-prep/exam quality, family/hereditary risk and whether the colonoscopy was otherwise complete. Use the current provincial/endoscopy surveillance pathway and do not substitute FIT for a colonoscopy surveillance indication.
recognize: Adenoma, sessile serrated lesion, advanced histology, large size, multiplicity and incomplete/uncertain resection increase future-neoplasia concern.
A high-quality negative or low-risk examination supports a longer interval than an advanced or technically inadequate examination.
differentiate: Average-risk population screening is different from post-polypectomy surveillance.
A positive FIT after a prior polyp history still requires the appropriate diagnostic/endoscopic pathway; it does not reset the surveillance clock by itself.
assessment: Obtain the actual colonoscopy and pathology reports, including size, number, histology, prep quality, cecal intubation/completeness and resection method.
Clarify family history, IBD and hereditary-cancer syndromes that may override routine post-polypectomy intervals.
workup: Do not choose an interval from the patient's memory that 'a few polyps were removed'; retrieve pathology/endoscopy details.
Use the current regional/provincial surveillance pathway because Canadian post-polypectomy recommendations and implementation can change.
management: Schedule surveillance according to the highest-risk relevant finding and endoscopic quality.
Early repeat endoscopy is appropriate when resection was piecemeal/incomplete or the examination was inadequate, according to endoscopy guidance.
Refer unusual polyposis burden or hereditary-pattern findings for genetic/high-risk assessment.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural anticoagulant/antiplatelet management depends on the planned intervention and thrombotic risk; use current endoscopy guidance.
Avoid unnecessary medication interruption for a low-risk diagnostic procedure when the current protocol does not require it.
redFlags: New GI bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia between surveillance exams
Poor-quality prior examination with missed-lesion concern
counselling: Explain that surveillance timing is based on what the pathology and quality of the last colonoscopy showed, not on symptoms alone.
followUp: Document the next interval and responsibility for recall; new alarm symptoms switch from surveillance to diagnostic evaluation.
examTrap: Telling every patient with any removed polyp to repeat colonoscopy in five years without reading the pathology report.
oneLinePearl: Polyp surveillance is a pathology-and-quality decision, not a memorized interval.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology endoscopy guideline library — post-polypectomy guideline currently under redevelopment

title: Chronic Constipation: Define the Pattern Before Adding More Laxatives
bottomLine: Chronic constipation is evaluated by stool frequency/form, straining, incomplete evacuation and defecatory symptoms plus medication and alarm-feature review. Most younger low-risk patients do not need colonoscopy solely for constipation; treat reversible causes and escalate to anorectal/colonic testing when symptoms suggest defecatory dysfunction or refractory disease.
recognize: Constipation may mean infrequent stool, hard stool, straining or incomplete evacuation rather than frequency alone.
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, some antihypertensives, low mobility, dehydration and neurologic/endocrine disease are common contributors.
differentiate: Defecatory disorder is suggested by excessive straining, digital maneuvers, blockage sensation or failed laxative therapy and may need pelvic-floor/anorectal testing.
Obstruction, cancer, severe hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia and neurologic disease are not 'functional constipation' when the clinical clues support them.
assessment: Review stool pattern, diet/fibre/fluid, activity, medications, pregnancy, neurologic symptoms, pelvic-floor symptoms, bleeding, anemia, weight loss and family history.
Perform abdominal and rectal examination when clinically indicated.
workup: Use targeted CBC/TSH/calcium or other tests only when history/exam suggests a secondary cause.
Choosing Wisely Canada advises against colonoscopy for constipation in younger patients without family history or alarm features; age-appropriate CRC screening is a separate issue.
Use anorectal manometry/balloon expulsion or colonic-transit testing for appropriately selected refractory patterns.
management: Start with adequate fibre when appropriate, osmotic laxative therapy and individualized behaviour/activity strategies.
Use stimulant/secretagogue/prokinetic options according to symptoms and current constipation guidance when first-line therapy is insufficient.
Pelvic-floor biofeedback is preferred for confirmed defecatory dysfunction rather than escalating oral laxatives indefinitely.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic unnecessary magnesium/phosphate products in renal impairment and review electrolyte risk from overuse.
Opioid-induced constipation requires a medication-specific prevention/treatment plan and sometimes peripheral opioid-antagonist therapy.
redFlags: New severe constipation with neurologic deficit
counselling: Set realistic bowel goals and explain that daily bowel movements are not required for health.
followUp: Reassess response, adherence and defecatory symptoms; refractory disease should trigger phenotype reassessment rather than simply stacking laxatives.
examTrap: Ordering colonoscopy solely for longstanding constipation in a younger low-risk patient with no alarm features.
oneLinePearl: Constipation management starts by identifying whether the problem is stool consistency, transit, or evacuation.

title: Chronic Diarrhea: Inflammatory, Malabsorptive, Secretory, Medication, or Functional?
bottomLine: Chronic diarrhea requires pattern-based evaluation rather than a universal stool-test panel. Define duration, nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight loss, medication/travel/exposure history and whether the process appears inflammatory, fatty/malabsorptive, watery or functional; alarm features and objective inflammation change the urgency toward colonoscopy or specialist evaluation.
recognize: Inflammatory diarrhea may include blood, urgency, fever, nocturnal symptoms and inflammatory markers; malabsorption can cause weight loss, nutrient deficiency and bulky/fatty stool.
Microscopic colitis can cause chronic watery diarrhea with normal-appearing colon and requires biopsy for diagnosis.
differentiate: IBS-D lacks objective inflammatory/alarm features, although symptoms can be severe.
Medication causes include metformin, magnesium, antibiotics, PPIs, SSRIs and others; bile-acid diarrhea and celiac disease are frequently missed treatable causes.
assessment: Assess stool characteristics/frequency, nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight, diet, travel/water exposures, medications, prior surgery, immune status, family IBD/celiac/cancer history and endocrine symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function, celiac testing, CRP/fecal calprotectin and stool infectious testing selectively based on phenotype and risk.
Use colonoscopy with biopsies for alarm/inflammatory features, persistent unexplained watery diarrhea or age/risk indications; do not assume a visually normal colon excludes microscopic colitis.
Consider bile-acid diarrhea testing/therapeutic pathway according to current CAG guidance.
management: Treat the identified cause and correct dehydration/nutritional deficits.
Avoid chronic empiric antidiarrheal therapy when inflammatory, infectious or obstructive disease remains plausible.
medicationSafety: Loperamide and similar agents can be dangerous in severe inflammatory/infectious colitis or ileus/toxic megacolon concern.
Review medication withdrawal/substitution before adding new therapies when a likely drug cause exists.
counselling: Explain why targeted testing is more useful than ordering every available stool assay and provide dehydration/alarm return precautions.
followUp: Close the loop on pathology/celiac/infectious studies and reassess persistent symptoms after an empiric treatment only if the original diagnostic hypothesis was reasonable.
examTrap: Calling chronic watery diarrhea IBS because colonoscopy looked normal without obtaining biopsies when microscopic colitis is plausible.
oneLinePearl: Classify chronic diarrhea by pattern before you order the panel.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline resources including bile acid diarrhea

title: GI Bleeding: Stabilize Perfusion, Localize the Source, Then Use Endoscopy Strategically
bottomLine: GI bleeding is a hemodynamic problem before it is an endoscopy problem. Assess airway and perfusion, establish IV access and appropriate laboratory/blood-bank support, resuscitate and reverse relevant anticoagulation only when indicated, then use risk-stratified endoscopy/other localization to achieve source control.
recognize: Hematemesis/melena usually suggests upper GI bleeding; hematochezia may be lower GI but brisk upper bleeding can also present this way.
Initial hemoglobin may not reflect the full acute blood loss before equilibration; vital signs/perfusion and trend matter.
differentiate: Variceal bleeding requires a cirrhosis/portal-hypertension pathway with vasoactive therapy/antibiotics and urgent endoscopy.
Stable occult blood/iron-deficiency anemia is different from active hemodynamically significant hemorrhage.
assessment: Assess airway, mental status, orthostasis/hemodynamics, ongoing bleeding, cirrhosis, NSAIDs, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, prior ulcer/bleed and comorbidity.
Estimate severity/risk and ask whether the patient can safely undergo urgent endoscopy or needs higher-level stabilization first.
workup: Use CBC, type/screen or crossmatch, renal/electrolytes, INR/coagulation in relevant patients and other labs guided by liver/cardiac context.
Upper endoscopy is central for significant upper GI bleed after stabilization; colonoscopy/CTA/interventional radiology strategy for lower bleeding depends on stability and ongoing hemorrhage.
management: Use balanced resuscitation and restrictive transfusion principles in most stable patients while individualizing for shock/ischemia/comorbidity.
Give IV PPI in appropriate suspected nonvariceal upper bleeding and manage variceal bleeding with the acute cirrhosis pathway.
Achieve endoscopic/radiologic/surgical source control rather than repeatedly transfusing without controlling the lesion.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant reversal depends on bleeding severity, drug and thrombotic risk; do not reverse minor bleeding reflexively or leave high-thrombotic-risk patients off therapy indefinitely after hemostasis.
NSAIDs and ulcerogenic combinations require review.
counselling: After stabilization, explain the bleeding source, medication changes and concrete return precautions.
followUp: Ensure pathology/H. pylori results, antithrombotic resumption, iron replacement and repeat endoscopy needs are closed-loop.
examTrap: Waiting for the hemoglobin to fall before treating a hypotensive patient with obvious active GI hemorrhage.
oneLinePearl: In GI bleeding, perfusion and source control outrank the first hemoglobin number.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology upper-GI bleeding and antithrombotic/periendoscopic guidelines

title: Dysphagia: Oropharyngeal or Esophageal Before You Order the Test
bottomLine: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom. First localize it: difficulty initiating a swallow with coughing/choking suggests oropharyngeal disease, while food sticking after swallowing suggests esophageal disease. Progressive solids-to-liquids dysphagia, weight loss, anemia or impaction requires urgent structural evaluation rather than empiric GERD treatment alone.
recognize: Oropharyngeal dysphagia can cause coughing, choking, wet voice, nasal regurgitation or aspiration and is common after stroke or neuromuscular disease.
Esophageal dysphagia can be mechanical/structural or motility related; solids-only progressive disease suggests obstruction, while solids and liquids from onset can suggest motility disease.
differentiate: Globus without true impaired transit is different from dysphagia.
Eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, cancer, rings/webs and achalasia/motility disorders require different testing/treatment.
assessment: Clarify initiation vs transit, solids vs liquids, progression, impaction, aspiration, neurologic disease, reflux, atopy, weight loss, bleeding/anemia and medication injury.
workup: Oropharyngeal symptoms require swallowing/SLP assessment and appropriate instrumental study when aspiration risk matters.
Esophageal dysphagia generally requires upper endoscopy with biopsy as appropriate; barium/esophageal manometry are selected for structural/motility questions after the initial pathway.
management: Treat aspiration risk immediately with appropriate diet/feeding/swallowing strategy while cause is evaluated.
Endoscopically treat dilation/impaction/structural disease when indicated and refer malignancy or significant motility disease appropriately.
medicationSafety: Avoid oral medications/food when severe oropharyngeal dysphagia makes swallowing unsafe until an appropriate route/plan is established.
Pill esophagitis risk increases with certain drugs and inadequate water/recumbency.
counselling: Teach aspiration precautions and explain why dysphagia deserves structural/neurologic evaluation rather than being assumed to be reflux.
followUp: Close pathology/endoscopy/manometry/swallow-study results and reassess nutrition/weight and aspiration risk.
examTrap: Treating progressive solid-food dysphagia with another PPI trial without endoscopic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Localize dysphagia before testing: mouth/pharynx or esophagus changes the entire pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology dysphagia/endoscopy practice resources

title: Anorectal Symptoms: Do Not Call Every Rectal Bleed Hemorrhoids
bottomLine: Hemorrhoids, fissure, abscess/fistula, proctitis and malignancy can all produce anorectal symptoms. Use history plus inspection/digital/anoscopy when appropriate, confirm the actual lesion and still apply age/risk/alarm-feature colorectal evaluation rather than attributing bleeding automatically to hemorrhoids.
recognize: Internal hemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red bleeding/prolapse; fissure causes severe pain with defecation and a tear; perianal abscess causes focal severe pain/swelling and may have fever.
Proctitis can cause urgency, pain, bleeding or discharge and may be inflammatory or infectious.
differentiate: Colorectal cancer, IBD, rectal prolapse, STI/proctitis and dermatologic disease can mimic common benign anorectal disorders.
A tender thrombosed external hemorrhoid differs from uncomplicated internal hemorrhoidal bleeding.
assessment: Assess bleeding amount/pattern, pain, bowel habits, constipation/straining, pregnancy, anticoagulants, sexual/STI risk, weight/anemia/family history and systemic symptoms.
workup: Perform appropriate anorectal examination/anoscopy when safe and useful.
Use colonoscopy or other evaluation when age/risk/alarm features require it; visible hemorrhoids do not automatically explain iron-deficiency anemia or persistent bleeding.
management: Treat constipation/fibre/straining and local hemorrhoidal symptoms conservatively first when uncomplicated.
Fissure treatment targets stool consistency and sphincter relaxation; abscess generally requires drainage rather than oral antibiotics alone.
Refer persistent high-grade prolapse, recurrent significant bleeding, fistula or uncertain lesions to colorectal care.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged unsupervised topical steroid/anesthetic use and review bleeding risk in anticoagulated patients.
Antibiotics do not replace drainage for a drainable anorectal abscess except where specific indications coexist.
counselling: Normalize discussion of anorectal symptoms and provide bowel-habit strategies without assuming symptoms are benign.
followUp: Reassess ongoing bleeding/pain after initial treatment and ensure cancer/IBD/STI pathways are completed when indicated.
examTrap: Stopping the workup of recurrent rectal bleeding because hemorrhoids are visible on examination.
oneLinePearl: Hemorrhoids can bleed—but seeing them does not prove they are the only diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society colorectal diagnostic resources

title: Acute Abdominal Pain: Disposition Before Diagnostic Perfection
bottomLine: Acute abdominal pain is a disposition problem before it is a final-diagnosis problem. Identify shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, obstruction, ischemia, perforation, appendicitis, biliary/pancreatic disease and dangerous extra-abdominal mimics, then choose testing and imaging from the differential rather than ordering a universal abdominal panel or CT.
recognize: Peritonitis, rigidity/involuntary guarding, pain out of proportion, GI bleeding, persistent bilious/feculent vomiting, fever with toxicity or hemodynamic instability are high-risk findings.
Older adults and immunocompromised patients may have muted tenderness/fever despite serious disease.
differentiate: Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, gynecologic and genitourinary disease can present as abdominal pain.
Symptom improvement after analgesia does not prove the cause is benign.
assessment: Assess ABCs/hemodynamics, onset/location/migration, vomiting/stool/urine, bleeding, fever, prior surgery, medications/NSAIDs/anticoagulants and pregnancy possibility.
Perform focused abdominal plus relevant pelvic/testicular/cardiopulmonary/vascular examination.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal, liver/pancreatic tests, urinalysis, pregnancy test, ECG/troponin or imaging only when they answer the differential.
Use ultrasound preferentially for many biliary/pelvic/pregnancy questions and CT when the suspected pathology/urgency justifies it.
management: Give appropriate analgesia/antiemetics while evaluating; pain treatment does not prevent diagnosis.
Escalate suspected peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, compromised obstruction, ectopic pregnancy, AAA or hemodynamic instability to emergency/surgical care.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs may worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids require sedation/respiratory monitoring but should not be withheld from severe pain solely to preserve the exam.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics when no bacterial/surgical infection syndrome exists.
counselling: For safe outpatient cases, give explicit return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding, syncope or inability to hydrate.
followUp: Ensure pending imaging/labs and evolving diagnoses have a defined review plan; recurrent undiagnosed pain should not receive repeated empiric therapy without reassessment.
examTrap: Ordering CT immediately for every abdominal pain before checking pregnancy, hemodynamics and a focused differential.
oneLinePearl: Abdominal pain: first decide who is unsafe, then decide which test answers why.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency/primary-care abdominal pain practice principles
